claim: The cerebellum integrates sensory stimuli and motor actions to enable smooth coordination and motor learning.
source: The cerebellum integrates sensory stimuli and motor actions to enable smooth coordination and motor learning.
evidence: This is a well-established principle in neuroscience supported by extensive literature.

claim: Population imaging reveals three spatially-clustered regions of Purkinje cell activity along the rostrocaudal axis.
source: Population imaging reveals three spatially-clustered regions of Purkinje cell activity along the rostrocaudal axis.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from population imaging experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Purkinje cells can be assigned to one of three functional phenotypes that encode a specific visual, and not motor, signal via complex spikes.
source: Complementary single-cell electrophysiological recordings assign these Purkinje cells to one of three functional phenotypes that encode a specific visual, and not motor, signal via complex spikes.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings and multilinear regression analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Simple spike output of most Purkinje cells is strongly driven by motor-related tail and eye signals.
source: In contrast, simple spike output of most Purkinje cells is strongly driven by motor-related tail and eye signals.
evidence: This is demonstrated through electrophysiological recordings and multilinear regression analysis.

claim: Interactions between complex and simple spikes show heterogeneous modulation patterns across different Purkinje cells.
source: Interactions between complex and simple spikes show heterogeneous modulation patterns across different Purkinje cells, which become temporally restricted during swimming episodes.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of complex spike-simple spike relationships in the electrophysiological data.

claim: The modulation patterns between complex and simple spikes become temporally restricted during swimming episodes.
source: Interactions between complex and simple spikes show heterogeneous modulation patterns across different Purkinje cells, which become temporally restricted during swimming episodes.
evidence: This is demonstrated through analysis of motor context effects on complex spike-simple spike relationships.

claim: Purkinje cells receive two excitatory input streams, via parallel fibers from granule cells and a single climbing fiber from the inferior olive.
source: Purkinje cells receive two excitatory input streams, via parallel fibers from granule cells and a single climbing fiber from the inferior olive, that differentially modulate their spike output.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cerebellar anatomy and physiology.

claim: Climbing fibers from inferior olivary neurons drive complex spikes in Purkinje cells at a spontaneous rate of ~0.5–2 Hz.
source: Across vertebrate species, climbing fibers from inferior olivary neurons drive complex spikes in Purkinje cells at a spontaneous rate of ~0.5–2 Hz whereas parallel fiber inputs modulate intrinsic simple spike activity at much higher rates (from tens of Hz in larval zebrafish up to hundreds of Hz in mammals; Hsieh et al., 2014; Eccles et al., 1967; Raman and Bean, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Parallel fiber inputs modulate intrinsic simple spike activity at much higher rates, from tens of Hz in larval zebrafish up to hundreds of Hz in mammals.
source: Across vertebrate species, climbing fibers from inferior olivary neurons drive complex spikes in Purkinje cells at a spontaneous rate of ~0.5–2 Hz whereas parallel fiber inputs modulate intrinsic simple spike activity at much higher rates (from tens of Hz in larval zebrafish up to hundreds of Hz in mammals; Hsieh et al., 2014; Eccles et al., 1967; Raman and Bean, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Simple spike output can be biased to burst or pause by the arrival of a complex spike.
source: Simple spike output can furthermore be biased to burst or pause by the arrival of a complex spike (Mathews et al., 2012; Badura et al., 2013; Sengupta and Thirumalai, 2015), though the precise nature of this relationship varies across Purkinje cells (Zhou et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2015; Xiao et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The precise nature of the complex spike-simple spike relationship varies across Purkinje cells.
source: Simple spike output can furthermore be biased to burst or pause by the arrival of a complex spike (Mathews et al., 2012; Badura et al., 2013; Sengupta and Thirumalai, 2015), though the precise nature of this relationship varies across Purkinje cells (Zhou et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2015; Xiao et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Inhibitory interneurons may exert considerable control over simple spike rates.
source: In addition, inhibitory interneurons may also exert considerable control over simple spike rates (Dizon and Khodakhah, 2011; ten Brinke et al., 2015; Jelitai et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The rat cerebellum contains more than 300,000 Purkinje cells.
source: Characterizing the type of information carried by these different input streams at the population level and disentangling their relative contributions to Purkinje cell output has been challenging due to the large number of Purkinje cells in the mammalian cerebellum (>300,000 in the rat cerebellum) receiving convergent input from 100,000 to 200,000 parallel fibers (Harvey and Napper, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Each Purkinje cell in the rat cerebellum receives convergent input from 100,000 to 200,000 parallel fibers.
source: Characterizing the type of information carried by these different input streams at the population level and disentangling their relative contributions to Purkinje cell output has been challenging due to the large number of Purkinje cells in the mammalian cerebellum (>300,000 in the rat cerebellum) receiving convergent input from 100,000 to 200,000 parallel fibers (Harvey and Napper, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Four transverse zones along the rostrocaudal axis have been described in the mammalian cerebellum.
source: Four transverse zones along the rostrocaudal axis have been described (Ozol et al., 1999) that can be further subdivided into longitudinal zones and microzones defined by additional anatomical, physiological and molecular features (see Apps and Hawkes, 2009 for review).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cerebellar zones can be further subdivided into longitudinal zones and microzones defined by additional anatomical, physiological and molecular features.
source: Four transverse zones along the rostrocaudal axis have been described (Ozol et al., 1999) that can be further subdivided into longitudinal zones and microzones defined by additional anatomical, physiological and molecular features (see Apps and Hawkes, 2009 for review).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cerebellar organization is thought to produce functional modules that each participate in the control of a certain set of behaviors.
source: This organization is thought to produce functional modules that each participate in the control of a certain set of behaviors (Cerminara and Apps, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The larval zebrafish cerebellum is anatomically organized in a typical vertebrate tri-layered configuration.
source: The larval zebrafish cerebellum is anatomically organized in a typical vertebrate tri-layered configuration, with a population of fewer than 500 Purkinje cells, each receiving inputs from many parallel fibers and likely just one climbing fiber (Bae et al., 2009; Hashimoto and Hibi, 2012; Hsieh et al., 2014; Hamling et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The larval zebrafish cerebellum contains a population of fewer than 500 Purkinje cells.
source: The larval zebrafish cerebellum is anatomically organized in a typical vertebrate tri-layered configuration, with a population of fewer than 500 Purkinje cells, each receiving inputs from many parallel fibers and likely just one climbing fiber (Bae et al., 2009; Hashimoto and Hibi, 2012; Hsieh et al., 2014; Hamling et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Each Purkinje cell in larval zebrafish receives inputs from many parallel fibers and likely just one climbing fiber.
source: The larval zebrafish cerebellum is anatomically organized in a typical vertebrate tri-layered configuration, with a population of fewer than 500 Purkinje cells, each receiving inputs from many parallel fibers and likely just one climbing fiber (Bae et al., 2009; Hashimoto and Hibi, 2012; Hsieh et al., 2014; Hamling et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The cerebellum in larval zebrafish has a functional role relating to motor coordination, adaptation, and learning.
source: Several studies have demonstrated a functional role for the cerebellum in the larval zebrafish relating to motor coordination, adaptation, and learning (Aizenberg and Schuman, 2011; Ahrens et al., 2012; Matsui et al., 2014; Portugues et al., 2014; Harmon et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The behavioral repertoire of larval zebrafish includes robust but variable swimming and eye movements to drifting gratings and rotating stimuli.
source: The behavioral repertoire of the larval zebrafish includes robust but variable swimming and eye movements to drifting gratings and rotating stimuli (the optomotor and optokinetic response, respectively).
evidence: This is established knowledge about zebrafish behavior.

claim: Visual stimuli elicit graded, episodic swim bouts and eye movements that vary across trials in larval zebrafish.
source: These visual stimuli are particularly useful because they elicit graded, episodic swim bouts and eye movements that vary across trials, allowing us to disambiguate clearly between sensory and motor responses.
evidence: This is based on observations from the experimental data in this study.

claim: Whole-field gratings moving in the four cardinal directions elicited reflexive but variable optomotor swimming responses.
source: Whole-field gratings moving in the four cardinal directions elicited reflexive but variable optomotor swimming responses.
evidence: This is based on behavioral observations during the experiments.

claim: Swimming episodes were evoked in a probabilistic manner that was modulated by the direction and speed of visual motion.
source: Swimming episodes (bouts) were evoked in a probabilistic manner that was modulated by the direction and speed of the visual motion (i.e. no swim response to gratings in the reverse direction).
evidence: This is based on behavioral observations during the experiments.

claim: A windmill pattern rotating with sinusoidal velocity elicited a reflexive optokinetic response of the eyes that showed behavioral variability across trials.
source: A windmill pattern centered on the larva's head rotating with a sinusoidal velocity elicited a reflexive optokinetic response of the eyes that also showed some behavioral variability across trials.
evidence: This is based on behavioral observations during the experiments.

claim: Moderate intensity whole-field flashes evoke no acute behavioral response in larval zebrafish.
source: Moderate intensity whole-field flashes were included to provide stimuli that evoke no acute behavioral response (Figure 1b) but that could nonetheless contribute to ethological behaviors over longer timescales, for example relating to circadian rhythms (Burgess and Granato, 2007).
evidence: This is based on behavioral observations during the experiments and supported by a citation.

claim: The number of Purkinje cells in the larval zebrafish at seven dpf is 433 ± 19.
source: We estimated the number of Purkinje cells in the larval zebrafish to be 433 ± 19 (mean ± std, N = 3) by identifying spherical nuclei in confocal stacks of a transgenic line that expresses nuclear-localized GCaMP6s using 3D template matching (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of confocal imaging data.

claim: The estimated number of Purkinje cells at seven dpf (433 ± 19) is higher than the previously reported range of 180–360 Purkinje cells.
source: This number is higher than the previously reported range of 180–360 Purkinje cells at seven dpf (N = 6; Hamling et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a comparison between the current study's data and previous literature.

claim: Purkinje cell activity is functionally segregated across the cerebellum with respect to different visual and motor features.
source: Our analysis showed that Purkinje cell activity is functionally segregated across the cerebellum with respect to different visual and motor features (Figure 2a, Video 3).
evidence: This is based on multilinear regression analysis of imaging data.

claim: Responses to whole-field flashes were enriched in a bilaterally symmetric central region of the cerebellar cortex.
source: Responses to whole-field flashes were enriched in a bilaterally symmetric central region of the cerebellar cortex, whereas responses to clockwise and counterclockwise rotational motion had an asymmetric localization within the left and right hemisphere of the caudolateral cerebellum, respectively.
evidence: This is based on analysis of imaging data showing spatial patterns of activity.

claim: Responses to clockwise and counterclockwise rotational motion had an asymmetric localization within the left and right hemisphere of the caudolateral cerebellum, respectively.
source: Responses to whole-field flashes were enriched in a bilaterally symmetric central region of the cerebellar cortex, whereas responses to clockwise and counterclockwise rotational motion had an asymmetric localization within the left and right hemisphere of the caudolateral cerebellum, respectively.
evidence: This is based on analysis of imaging data showing spatial patterns of activity.

claim: Purkinje cell responses to motor activity, including eye and tail motion, were generally broad and showed strong, uniform correlations across most of the cerebellar cortex.
source: Purkinje cell responses to motor activity, including eye and tail motion, were generally broad and showed strong, uniform correlations across most of the cerebellar cortex.
evidence: This is based on analysis of imaging data showing spatial patterns of activity.

claim: The activity of Purkinje cells distributed across a broad region of the cerebellum correlated highly with tail movement during swimming.
source: As Figure 2bi shows, the activity of Purkinje cells distributed across a broad region of the cerebellum correlated highly with tail movement during swimming and accounted for the modulation of calcium activity to a much greater extent that sensory grating motion.
evidence: This is based on analysis of imaging data and multilinear regression.

claim: Tail movement accounted for the modulation of Purkinje cell calcium activity to a much greater extent than sensory grating motion.
source: As Figure 2bi shows, the activity of Purkinje cells distributed across a broad region of the cerebellum correlated highly with tail movement during swimming and accounted for the modulation of calcium activity to a much greater extent that sensory grating motion.
evidence: This is based on multilinear regression analysis comparing sensory and motor contributions.

claim: A large dense bilateral area of the caudolateral cerebellum had activity that was more strongly related to sensory rotational motion.
source: In contrast, Figure 2bii shows that a large dense bilateral area of the caudolateral cerebellum had activity that was more strongly related to sensory rotational motion while the remaining area of the rostral and medial cerebellum showed a stronger correlation with eye movements.
evidence: This is based on analysis of imaging data comparing sensory and motor contributions.

claim: The remaining area of the rostral and medial cerebellum showed a stronger correlation with eye movements than with sensory rotational motion.
source: In contrast, Figure 2bii shows that a large dense bilateral area of the caudolateral cerebellum had activity that was more strongly related to sensory rotational motion while the remaining area of the rostral and medial cerebellum showed a stronger correlation with eye movements.
evidence: This is based on analysis of imaging data comparing sensory and motor contributions.

claim: Locomotor activity of the tail and eyes is broadly encoded in Purkinje cell activity across the cerebellum.
source: These results indicate that locomotor activity of the tail and eyes is broadly encoded in Purkinje cell activity across the cerebellum whereas sensory responses to visual features are more anatomically clustered.
evidence: This is an inference based on the imaging data analysis.

claim: Sensory responses to visual features are more anatomically clustered than motor responses.
source: These results indicate that locomotor activity of the tail and eyes is broadly encoded in Purkinje cell activity across the cerebellum whereas sensory responses to visual features are more anatomically clustered.
evidence: This is an inference based on the imaging data analysis.

claim: Four functional clusters emerged that were particularly spatially-clustered and tiled the cerebellum across the rostrocaudal axis of each hemisphere.
source: Four functional clusters emerged that were particularly spatially-clustered and tiled the cerebellum across the rostrocaudal axis of each hemisphere (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is based on principal component analysis of imaging data.

claim: Every complex spike elicited a peak in the calcium signal of a Purkinje cell's dendrites.
source: As expected, we found that every complex spike elicited a peak in the calcium signal of a Purkinje cell's dendrites (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a,b).
evidence: This is based on simultaneous electrophysiology and calcium imaging experiments.

claim: Isolated bursts of simple spikes correlated with widespread increases in the dendritic calcium signal.
source: However, we also found that isolated bursts of simple spikes correlated with widespread increases in the dendritic calcium signal.
evidence: This is based on simultaneous electrophysiology and calcium imaging experiments.

claim: Simple spike-triggered calcium transients were of smaller amplitude but similar duration to complex spike-triggered transients.
source: Aligning the calcium signal to the onset of simple spike bursts and single complex spike events showed consistent simple spike-triggered calcium transients that were of smaller amplitude but similar duration to complex spike-triggered transients (Figure 1—figure supplement 2b,d).
evidence: This is based on analysis of simultaneous electrophysiology and calcium imaging data.

claim: The majority of the calcium signal in Purkinje cells is driven by the occurrence of a complex spike.
source: We find that although the majority of the signal is driven by the occurrence of a complex spike, simple spikes also contribute to a varying degree across cells and can account for up to half of the calcium signal (mean percentage contribution from complex spikes = 78.4 ± 6.8%, N = 8 cells from eight fish; Figure 1—figure supplement 2e,f).
evidence: This is based on multilinear regression analysis of simultaneous electrophysiology and calcium imaging data.

claim: Simple spikes can account for up to half of the calcium signal in some Purkinje cells.
source: We find that although the majority of the signal is driven by the occurrence of a complex spike, simple spikes also contribute to a varying degree across cells and can account for up to half of the calcium signal (mean percentage contribution from complex spikes = 78.4 ± 6.8%, N = 8 cells from eight fish; Figure 1—figure supplement 2e,f).
evidence: This is based on multilinear regression analysis of simultaneous electrophysiology and calcium imaging data.

claim: Somatic signals and dendritic signals in Purkinje cells were highly correlated with each other (mean correlation = 0.87 ± 0.2).
source: We furthermore observed that somatic signals and dendritic signals were highly correlated with each other (mean correlation = 0.87 ± 0.2, N = 5 cells from three fish; Figure 1—figure supplement 2g,h), suggesting that the contribution from these different input streams may not be as spatially segregated in these Purkinje cells as shown in other systems and therefore cannot be isolated by subcellular imaging.
evidence: This is based on analysis of calcium imaging data from different subcellular compartments.

claim: Calcium signals across Purkinje cells report both complex spikes and high frequency simple spiking.
source: In summary, calcium signals across Purkinje cells report both complex spikes and high frequency simple spiking and care must therefore be taken when interpreting the underlying activity patterns of Purkinje cells measured with functional imaging.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined electrophysiology and calcium imaging experiments.

claim: Swimming activity is only moderately correlated with forward visual motion on a trial by trial basis (mean correlation = 0.31 ± 0.2).
source: For example, we find that swimming activity is only moderately correlated with forward visual motion on a trial by trial basis (mean correlation = 0.31 ± 0.2, Figure 3c, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on analysis of behavioral data during electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Complex spikes were generally evoked by a narrow subset of stimuli.
source: We observed that complex spikes were generally evoked by a narrow subset of stimuli.
evidence: This is based on analysis of electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Only a few visual or motor features provided a significant contribution to each cell's complex spike rate (mean number of nonzero coefficients = 6.0 ± 0.4 out of 22).
source: Only a few visual or motor features provided a significant contribution to each cell's complex spike rate (mean number of nonzero coefficients = 6.0 ± 0.4 out of 22, N = 61), and in many cases a single feature was very dominant (Figure 3e).
evidence: This is based on multilinear regression analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: In many Purkinje cells, a single feature was very dominant in driving complex spike responses.
source: Only a few visual or motor features provided a significant contribution to each cell's complex spike rate (mean number of nonzero coefficients = 6.0 ± 0.4 out of 22, N = 61), and in many cases a single feature was very dominant (Figure 3e).
evidence: This is based on multilinear regression analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: There is little evidence that individual Purkinje cells encode multiple types of visual stimuli or both visual and motor features in their complex spike responses.
source: We found little evidence however that individual Purkinje cells encode multiple types of visual stimuli or both visual and motor features in their complex spike responses.
evidence: This is based on analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: Purkinje cell complex spike responses were strongly enriched for visual information.
source: A survey of the best regressor category for each cell from this dataset revealed that Purkinje cell complex spike responses were strongly enriched for visual information (Figure 3e), specifically the onset of direction-specific translational motion (N = 31/61) and direction-specific rotational velocity (N = 14/61).
evidence: This is based on multilinear regression analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: 31 out of 61 Purkinje cells had complex spike responses best explained by the onset of direction-specific translational motion.
source: A survey of the best regressor category for each cell from this dataset revealed that Purkinje cell complex spike responses were strongly enriched for visual information (Figure 3e), specifically the onset of direction-specific translational motion (N = 31/61) and direction-specific rotational velocity (N = 14/61).
evidence: This is based on multilinear regression analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: 14 out of 61 Purkinje cells had complex spike responses best explained by direction-specific rotational velocity.
source: A survey of the best regressor category for each cell from this dataset revealed that Purkinje cell complex spike responses were strongly enriched for visual information (Figure 3e), specifically the onset of direction-specific translational motion (N = 31/61) and direction-specific rotational velocity (N = 14/61).
evidence: This is based on multilinear regression analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: Sensory responses across visual features are far better represented than motor responses in the complex spike responses of Purkinje cells.
source: Notably, sensory responses across visual features are far better represented than motor responses in the complex spike responses of Purkinje cells (Figure 3e).
evidence: This is based on multilinear regression analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: Only 8 out of 61 cells had the biggest contribution to complex spike rates from motor activity.
source: Only 8/61 cells had the biggest contribution to complex spike rates from motor activity, and across the remaining cells the average contribution from motor regressors was less than 5% (3.7 ± 1%, N = 53).
evidence: This is based on multilinear regression analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: Across Purkinje cells without motor-dominant complex spikes, the average contribution from motor regressors was less than 5% (3.7 ± 1%).
source: Only 8/61 cells had the biggest contribution to complex spike rates from motor activity, and across the remaining cells the average contribution from motor regressors was less than 5% (3.7 ± 1%, N = 53).
evidence: This is based on multilinear regression analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: All but one of the Purkinje cells recorded from across the entire cerebellum could be unambiguously assigned to one of three visual complex spike phenotypes.
source: As a result, we made the surprising observation that all but one of the Purkinje cells that we recorded from across the entire cerebellum could be unambiguously assigned to one of three visual complex spike 'phenotypes' corresponding to a response to directionally-selective translational motion onset, directionally-selective rotational velocity, or changes in luminance.
evidence: This is based on comprehensive analysis of electrophysiological data from 61 cells.

claim: The three visual complex spike phenotypes correspond to responses to directionally-selective translational motion onset, directionally-selective rotational velocity, or changes in luminance.
source: As a result, we made the surprising observation that all but one of the Purkinje cells that we recorded from across the entire cerebellum could be unambiguously assigned to one of three visual complex spike 'phenotypes' corresponding to a response to directionally-selective translational motion onset, directionally-selective rotational velocity, or changes in luminance.
evidence: This is based on comprehensive analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: There is a spatial organization of complex spike sensory response phenotypes across the cerebellum.
source: Mapping the coordinates of all Purkinje cells onto a reference cerebellum revealed a spatial organization of complex spike sensory response phenotypes similar to our functional imaging data (Figure 3f).
evidence: This is based on mapping electrophysiological recording locations onto a reference brain.

claim: A rostromedial cluster of cells is responsive to the onset of directional motion in the visual stimulus.
source: In particular, we observed a rostromedial cluster of cells responsive to the onset of directional motion in the visual stimulus and a caudolateral cluster of cells responsive to rotational stimulus velocity.
evidence: This is based on spatial mapping of electrophysiological recordings.

claim: A caudolateral cluster of cells is responsive to rotational stimulus velocity.
source: In particular, we observed a rostromedial cluster of cells responsive to the onset of directional motion in the visual stimulus and a caudolateral cluster of cells responsive to rotational stimulus velocity.
evidence: This is based on spatial mapping of electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Luminance responses were more scattered but generally occupied the central zone between rostromedial and caudolateral regions.
source: Luminance responses were more scattered but generally occupied the central zone between these regions.
evidence: This is based on spatial mapping of electrophysiological recordings.

claim: The largest group of Purkinje cells (N = 33/61) showed a phenotype for strong, direction-selective responses to the onset of translational motion.
source: The largest group of Purkinje cells showed a phenotype for strong, direction-selective responses to the onset of translational motion (N = 33/61 cells).
evidence: This is based on analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: Direction-selective motion onset responses typically spanned two of the four cardinal directions tested, producing on average just one complex spike at the onset of motion in the preferred directions (1.2 ± 0.6 spikes/stimulus).
source: These responses typically spanned two of the four cardinal directions tested, producing on average just one complex spike at the onset of motion in the preferred directions (1.2 ± 0.6 spikes/stimulus; Figure 4a).
evidence: This is based on analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: The occurrence of a complex spike was not dependent on the behavioral response.
source: The occurrence of a complex spike was not dependent on the behavioral response since visually-evoked complex spikes occurred with equal probability whether there was a swimming response or not (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on analysis of electrophysiological and behavioral data.

claim: Reverse visual motion evokes no swimming but is equally well-represented by a complex spike response at motion onset as the directions that do drive swimming.
source: In the clearest example, reverse visual motion evokes no swimming but is equally well-represented by a complex spike response at motion onset as the directions that do drive swimming (Figures 3g and 4a, Figure 3—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is based on analysis of electrophysiological and behavioral data.

claim: The direction selectivity index of motion onset-responsive cells ranged from 0.2 to 0.9.
source: The direction selectivity index (see Materials and methods) of these cells ranged from 0.2 to 0.9 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a), and cells typically responded to two of the four cardinal directions tested (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: No cells were found that responded significantly to motion onset in opposing directions.
source: No cells were found that responded significantly to motion onset in opposing directions.
evidence: This is based on analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: Cells in the left cerebellar hemisphere preferred either forward motion to the right (0 to 90°, N = 7) or reverse motion to the left (−90 to −180°, N = 5).
source: Although the Purkinje cell somata displaying this complex spike phenotype were closely clustered in the most rostromedial part of the cerebellum (Figure 3f), the lateralization of Purkinje cells was biased such that cells in the left cerebellar hemisphere preferred either forward motion to the right (0 to 90°, N = 7) or reverse motion to the left (−90 to −180°, N = 5; Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is based on analysis of directional tuning in electrophysiological data.

claim: Purkinje cells in the right cerebellar hemisphere preferred either forward motion to the left (0 to −90°, N = 5) or reverse motion to the right (90 to 180°, N = 5).
source: Conversely, Purkinje cells in the right cerebellar hemisphere preferred either forward motion to the left (0 to −90°, N = 5) or reverse motion to the right (90 to 180°, N = 5; Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is based on analysis of directional tuning in electrophysiological data.

claim: The second group of Purkinje cells (N = 12/61) showed a phenotype for large, directionally-selective increase in complex spikes during either clockwise or counter-clockwise rotational motion that persisted throughout the duration of movement.
source: The second group of Purkinje cells, located in the caudolateral cerebellum, showed a phenotype for large, directionally-selective increase in complex spikes during either clockwise or counter-clockwise rotational motion that unlike the previous group persisted throughout the duration of movement (Figure 4b; N = 12/61 cells).
evidence: This is based on analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: During rotational motion in the preferred direction, complex spike firing rates in rotational motion-responsive cells were two to five times higher than baseline (mean rate increase = 340 ± 40%).
source: During rotational motion in the preferred direction, complex spike firing rates in these cells were two to five times higher than baseline (mean rate increase = 340 ± 40%, N = 12).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: Complex spike rates during motion in the non-preferred direction fell to nearly zero, well below the baseline rate (mean rate non-preferred direction = 0.32 ± 0.1 Hz versus 0.87 ± 0.1 Hz at baseline).
source: In contrast, complex spike rates during motion in the non-preferred direction fell to nearly zero, well below the baseline rate (mean rate non-preferred direction = 0.32 ± 0.1 Hz versus 0.87 ± 0.1 Hz at baseline; Figure 4—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: All Purkinje cells (10/10) that preferred clockwise rotational motion were located in the caudolateral region of the left cerebellar hemisphere.
source: Consistent with our functional imaging data (Figure 2), these complex spike responses to rotational motion were highly lateralized such that all Purkinje cells (10/10) that preferred clockwise rotational motion were located in the caudolateral region of the left cerebellar hemisphere while the only two Purkinje cells that preferred counter-clockwise motion were located in the mirror symmetric region of the right cerebellar hemisphere (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is based on spatial mapping of electrophysiological recordings.

claim: The only two Purkinje cells that preferred counter-clockwise motion were located in the mirror symmetric region of the right cerebellar hemisphere.
source: Consistent with our functional imaging data (Figure 2), these complex spike responses to rotational motion were highly lateralized such that all Purkinje cells (10/10) that preferred clockwise rotational motion were located in the caudolateral region of the left cerebellar hemisphere while the only two Purkinje cells that preferred counter-clockwise motion were located in the mirror symmetric region of the right cerebellar hemisphere (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is based on spatial mapping of electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Rotational motion-responsive Purkinje cells showed an increase in complex spiking for the duration of translational motion in a preferred lateral direction (mean rate increase above baseline = 280 ± 20%).
source: These Purkinje cells also showed an increase in complex spiking for the duration of translational motion in a preferred lateral direction, determined to be rightwards motion for clockwise motion-preferring cells and vice versa (mean rate increase above baseline = 280 ± 20%; Figure 4—figure supplement 1b), suggesting that these cells respond to motion over a large area situated in the front half of the visual field.
evidence: This is based on analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: Spontaneous complex spike rates in rotational motion-responsive cells were strongly depressed for several seconds following the robust complex spike responses elicited by rotational motion (normalized mean rate for one second following rotational stimuli = 37 ± 16% of spontaneous firing rates).
source: Finally, we observed an apparent homeostatic regulation firing in these cells where spontaneous complex spike rates were strongly depressed for several seconds following the robust complex spike responses elicited by rotational motion (normalized mean rate for one second following rotational stimuli = 37 ± 16% of spontaneous firing rates).
evidence: This is based on analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: The third prominent group of Purkinje cells (N = 25/61) had complex spike responses correlated with changes in whole-field luminance that were heterogeneous in feature encoding.
source: The third prominent group of Purkinje cells had complex spike responses correlated with changes in whole-field luminance that were surprisingly heterogeneous in feature encoding compared to the notably stereotyped responses seen for the previous two groups (N = 25/61 cells; Figure 4c and Figure 4—figure supplement 1c–e; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is based on analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: Purkinje cells with luminance phenotype had complex spike responses that encoded either luminance increases (9/25) or decreases (11/25) or both (5/25).
source: Purkinje cells with this luminance phenotype had complex spike responses that encoded either luminance increases (9/25) or decreases (11/25) or both (5/25; Figure 4c and Figure 4—figure supplement 1d) and the location of cells with different luminance response types was mixed across the central region of the cerebellum (Figure 4—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: This is based on analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: The location of cells with different luminance response types was mixed across the central region of the cerebellum.
source: Purkinje cells with this luminance phenotype had complex spike responses that encoded either luminance increases (9/25) or decreases (11/25) or both (5/25; Figure 4c and Figure 4—figure supplement 1d) and the location of cells with different luminance response types was mixed across the central region of the cerebellum (Figure 4—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: This is based on spatial mapping of electrophysiological recordings.

claim: The latency from the onset of the preferred luminance transition to the first complex spike occurred for each cell with very little jitter, but the latency itself varied across cells.
source: The latency from the onset of the preferred luminance transition to the first complex spike occurred for each cell with very little jitter, but the latency itself varied across cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is based on analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: Most whole-field luminance responses were transient such that cells fired just one complex spike for the preferred luminance change (mean = 0.80 ± 0.02 spikes).
source: Most whole-field luminance responses were transient such that cells fired just one complex spike for the preferred luminance change (mean = 0.80 ± 0.02 spikes).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: Two cells showed different complex firing rates as a function of the ambient luminance presented that did not adapt over tens of minutes.
source: We did however observe, in two cells, different complex firing rates as a function of the ambient luminance presented that did not adapt over tens of minutes and therefore appear to encode ambient luminance through their complex spike rate (Figure 4cii, one-way ANOVA with Bonferroni post hoc correction, p<0.01; Figure 4—figure supplement 1g,h).
evidence: This is based on analysis of electrophysiological data with statistical testing.

claim: Purkinje cells responding to rotational motion velocity had a significantly higher baseline firing rate than those with directionally selective motion onset responses (0.77 ± 0.1 Hz and 0.20 ± 0.02 Hz, respectively, p<0.001).
source: Purkinje cells responding to rotational motion velocity had a significantly higher baseline firing rate than those with directionally selective motion onset responses (0.77 ± 0.1 Hz and 0.20 ± 0.02 Hz, respectively, p<0.001, Bonferroni post hoc correction).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of electrophysiological data with statistical testing.

claim: Purkinje cells responding most strongly to luminance or motor activity had intermediate baseline complex spike rates (0.28 ± 0.1 Hz and 0.34 ± 0.1 Hz, respectively).
source: Purkinje cells responding most strongly to luminance or motor activity had intermediate baseline complex spike rates (0.28 ± 0.1 Hz and 0.34 ± 0.1 Hz, respectively).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: Zebrafish Purkinje cells can be divided into two anatomical populations - one with internally-projecting axons that contact eurydendroid cells and the other with externally-projecting caudal axons that contact neurons in the vestibular nuclei.
source: Unlike the mammalian cerebellum, where all Purkinje cell axons project outside of the cerebellar cortex, zebrafish Purkinje cells can be divided into two anatomical populations - one with internally-projecting axons that contact eurydendroid cells (the equivalent of mammalian cerebellar nuclei neurons) and the other whose somata are more lateral and who have externally-projecting caudal axons that contact neurons in the vestibular nuclei (Bae et al., 2009; Matsui et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: 6 out of 7 Purkinje cells with caudally projecting axons exhibited a clear complex spike phenotype for directional rotational motion.
source: Strikingly, 6/7 Purkinje cells with caudally projecting axons exhibited a clear complex spike phenotype for directional rotational motion, whereas only 1/10 cells with an internal axon had this same phenotype (Figure 4e).
evidence: This is based on combined electrophysiology and anatomical data.

claim: Only 1 out of 10 cells with an internal axon had a complex spike phenotype for directional rotational motion.
source: Strikingly, 6/7 Purkinje cells with caudally projecting axons exhibited a clear complex spike phenotype for directional rotational motion, whereas only 1/10 cells with an internal axon had this same phenotype (Figure 4e).
evidence: This is based on combined electrophysiology and anatomical data.

claim: Purkinje cell dendrites generally had a classic albeit simplified morphology with mostly planar dendrites.
source: We also found that Purkinje cell dendrites generally had a classic albeit simplified morphology with mostly planar dendrites (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) oriented orthogonally to the axis of parallel fiber extension across the cerebellum (Knogler et al., 2017), as seen in mammalian cerebellum (Eccles et al., 1967).
evidence: This is based on morphological analysis and supported by citations.

claim: Motor regressors did not significantly contribute to complex spike activity in the majority of Purkinje cells (N = 49/61).
source: As discussed above, motor regressors did not significantly contribute to complex spike activity in the majority of Purkinje cells (N = 49/61) despite an abundance of visually-evoked fictive behavior and the use of multiple motor regressors to capture different motor features.
evidence: This is based on multilinear regression analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: Some complex spikes were correlated with swimming activity even in the absence of visual stimuli.
source: We analyzed complex spike responses from Purkinje cells during spontaneously-evoked swimming in blank trials as well as in trials where visual stimuli elicited swimming and confirmed that some complex spikes were indeed correlated with swimming activity even in the absence of visual stimuli (Figure 4—figure supplement 3a).
evidence: This is based on analysis of electrophysiological data during blank trials.

claim: Swim-related complex spike responses were unreliable such that a complex spike occurred on fewer than half of swim bouts on average for motor-responsive cells (mean probability = 0.38 ± 0.07 for stimuli trials).
source: Swim-related responses were however unreliable such that a complex spike occurred on fewer than half of swim bouts on average for these cells (mean probability = 0.38 ± 0.07 for stimuli trials, N = 9 cells; mean probability for blank trials = 0.42 ± 0.07, N = 5 cells; p<0.05, Wilcoxon signed rank test).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of electrophysiological data with statistical testing.

claim: The latency from bout onset to the occurrence of a complex spike in blank trials varied considerably for an individual cell.
source: Aligning the subset of swim bouts that were positive for motor-related complex spikes showed that the latency from bout onset to the occurrence of a complex spike in blank trials varied considerably for an individual cell, in contrast to the fixed latencies for most visual-driven complex spikes (Figure 4—figure supplement 3b, compare with Figure 4 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: Complex spikes do not show phase-locking with stereotyped locomotor movements.
source: This is consistent with observations that complex spikes do not show phase-locking with stereotyped locomotor movements (Apps, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Purkinje cells with motor-related complex signals were distributed across the cerebellum with no apparent clustering.
source: Unlike the spatial mapping seen for Purkinje cells with visual complex spike responses, Purkinje cells with motor-related complex signals were distributed across the cerebellum with no apparent clustering (Figure 4—figure supplement 3e).
evidence: This is based on spatial mapping of electrophysiological recordings.

claim: The majority of Purkinje cells in the caudolateral region could be clearly assigned to a visual complex spike phenotype.
source: Nonetheless, the majority of Purkinje cells in this region could be clearly assigned to a visual complex spike phenotype since these cells showed very stereotyped complex spike responses to directional rotational stimuli that did not correlate well with the variable eye movements observed across trials (Figure 4—figure supplement 3j,k).
evidence: This is based on analysis of electrophysiological data from semi-paralyzed fish with eye tracking.

claim: Complex spike responses during rotational visual motion are predominantly sensory rather than motor.
source: We conclude from these data that the complex spike responses during rotational visual motion are predominantly sensory rather than motor.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on analysis of electrophysiological data with eye tracking.

claim: Many visual and motor features contributed to simple spike responses in individual Purkinje cells, such that response phenotypes were broader than those observed for complex spike activity.
source: Multilinear regression showed that many visual and motor features contributed to simple spike responses in individual Purkinje cells, such that response phenotypes were broader than those observed for complex spike activity (Figure 5a and Figure 3e), as expected in a circuit where many parallel fibers converge on a single Purkinje cell (De Zeeuw et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on multilinear regression analysis and supported by a citation.

claim: Motor activity significantly modulated simple spike activity in nearly all Purkinje cells across the cerebellum (N = 60/61).
source: Although simple spike rates were modulated to some extent by many of the visual stimuli presented, motor activity significantly modulated simple spike activity in nearly all Purkinje cells across the cerebellum (N = 60/61) and was in fact the main contributor to modulating simple spike activity in the majority of cells (N = 44/61; Figure 5a).
evidence: This is based on multilinear regression analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: Motor activity was the main contributor to modulating simple spike activity in the majority of cells (N = 44/61).
source: Although simple spike rates were modulated to some extent by many of the visual stimuli presented, motor activity significantly modulated simple spike activity in nearly all Purkinje cells across the cerebellum (N = 60/61) and was in fact the main contributor to modulating simple spike activity in the majority of cells (N = 44/61; Figure 5a).
evidence: This is based on multilinear regression analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: Simple spike firing rates had consistently larger contributions from swim vigor than from bout duration or any other motor regressor.
source: Simple spike firing rates for these cells had consistently larger contributions to their activity from swim vigor than from bout duration or any other motor regressor, suggesting that fictive swimming activity is encoded in a graded manner by simple spike output.
evidence: This is based on multilinear regression analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: Mean simple spike firing rates across the population were on average twice as high during a bout as during the rest of the trial (mean rate during a bout = 14.5 ± 1.5 Hz vs 7.6 ± 0.8 Hz at rest; p<0.001).
source: Mean simple spike firing rates across the population were on average twice as high during a bout as during the rest of the trial (mean rate during a bout = 14.5 ± 1.5 Hz vs 7.6 ± 0.8 Hz at rest; p<0.001, Wilcoxon signed rank test).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of electrophysiological data with statistical testing.

claim: Trial-averaged simple spike responses across the population appeared as a continuum rather than as clusters.
source: Trial-averaged simple spike responses across the population appeared as a continuum rather than as clusters (Figure 5b), suggesting that the organization of parallel fiber inputs does not follow the same regional specificity as climbing fiber inputs across the cerebellum.
evidence: This is based on analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: Translational and rotational motion of visual stimuli, regardless of direction, was the most prominent sensory feature encoded by simple spike activity.
source: Our analyses furthermore revealed that translational and rotational motion of visual stimuli, regardless of direction, was the most prominent sensory feature encoded by simple spike activity (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is based on multilinear regression analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: Fictive swim bouts consistently increased simple spike firing well above baseline levels.
source: Purkinje cells exhibit considerable spontaneous simple spike firing in the absence of any sensory stimuli or motor activity (Hsieh et al., 2014; Sengupta and Thirumalai, 2015); however fictive swim bouts consistently increased simple spike firing well above baseline levels (Figure 5c–e) and to an ever greater extent for spontaneous bouts in the absence of visual stimuli (p<0.01, Wilcoxon signed rank test).
evidence: This is based on analysis of electrophysiological data with statistical testing and supported by citations.

claim: The majority of Purkinje cells have consistent motor-related increases in simple spike activity that begin at bout onset and return to baseline following bout offset.
source: Aligning the mean bout-triggered simple spike rates for all Purkinje cells at bout onset and offset confirmed that the majority of cells have consistent motor-related increases in simple spike activity that begin at bout onset and return to baseline following bout offset (Figure 5e) although a small number of Purkinje cells instead show bout-triggered decreases in simple spike firing rates (Figure 5e), as observed elsewhere (Scalise et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on analysis of electrophysiological data and supported by a citation.

claim: The ventral root signal was highly autocorrelated for all fish with a mean autocorrelation frequency across fish of 26.7 ± 0.7 Hz.
source: As expected for rhythmic locomotor output, the ventral root signal was highly autocorrelated for all fish with a mean autocorrelation frequency across fish of 26.7 ± 0.7 Hz (N = 30 fish; Figure 5f), consistent with the slow swim bout frequency reported for restrained zebrafish larvae (Severi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on analysis of ventral root recordings and supported by a citation.

claim: Simple spikes in zebrafish Purkinje cells do not show significant autocorrelations at any frequency during spontaneous fictive bouts.
source: The autocorrelation analyses of simple spike firing for each Purkinje cell during a spontaneous fictive bout revealed however no significant autocorrelations for simple spikes at any frequency.
evidence: This is based on autocorrelation analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: Simple spikes in zebrafish Purkinje cells do not appear to be modulated in phase with rhythmic swimming activity but are nonetheless graded by swim strength.
source: Unlike the modulation of simple spike firing rate seen during step phase in locomoting rats (Sauerbrei et al., 2015), simple spikes in zebrafish Purkinje cells do not appear to be modulated in phase with rhythmic swimming activity but are nonetheless graded by swim strength.
evidence: This is based on analysis of electrophysiological data and comparison with literature.

claim: Individual Purkinje cell firing does not encode the activation of individual muscles involved in rhythmic swimming.
source: This suggests that individual Purkinje cell firing does not encode the activation of individual muscles involved in rhythmic swimming.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of phase-locking in simple spike activity.

claim: A disynaptic pathway from spinal premotor interneurons to the granule cells via the lateral reticular nucleus conveys information about ongoing network activity in the spinal cord.
source: A disynaptic pathway from spinal premotor interneurons to the granule cells via the lateral reticular nucleus was recently found that would convey information about ongoing network activity in the spinal cord (Pivetta et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: There is growing evidence across species that granule cells are strongly driven by ongoing locomotor activity.
source: There is growing evidence across species that granule cells are strongly driven by ongoing locomotor activity (Ozden et al., 2012; Powell et al., 2015; Jelitai et al., 2016; Giovannucci et al., 2017; Knogler et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In the electric fish, an overwhelming majority (>90%) of granule cells receive depolarizing motor efference signals during electric organ discharge, although this translated into spiking in only ~20% of granule cells.
source: Furthermore, extensive electrophysiological recordings from the granule cells of the cerebellum-like circuit of the electric organ in the electric fish revealed that an overwhelming majority (>90%) of granule cells receive depolarizing motor efference signals during electric organ discharge, although this translated into spiking in only ~20% of granule cells (Kennedy et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Granule cell activity was strong and widespread during swimming activity, both in the somatic layer and across the parallel fiber layer.
source: Across fish (N = 7), we observed that granule cell activity was strong and widespread during swimming activity, both in the somatic layer and across the parallel fiber layer (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is based on analysis of granule cell imaging data.

claim: Granule cell activity relating to eye movements was weaker but also widespread.
source: Granule cell activity relating to eye movements was weaker but also widespread (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is based on analysis of granule cell imaging data.

claim: A large number of granule cells receive mossy fiber inputs relaying motor efference copies that drive them to fire, and they in turn drive broad motor-related activation of simple spikes in Purkinje cells.
source: These findings suggest that a large number of granule cells receive mossy fiber inputs relaying motor efference copies that drive them to fire, and they in turn drive broad motor-related activation of simple spikes in Purkinje cells (Figure 2a,b).
evidence: This is an inference based on the imaging data.

claim: Several granule cells showed negligible firing rates in the absence of motor activity but large, significant increases in their spike rates during fictive bouts (N = 6/8 cells; mean firing rate at rest = 1.3 ± 0.3 Hz vs 25.7 ± 7.6 Hz during a bout; p<0.005).
source: These recordings revealed several granule cells with negligible firing rates in the absence of motor activity but that showed large, significant increases in their spike rates during fictive bouts (N = 6/8 cells; mean firing rate at rest = 1.3 ± 0.3 Hz vs 25.7 ± 7.6 Hz during a bout; p<0.005, Wilcoxon signed rank test; Figure 6b–d; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of electrophysiological data with statistical testing.

claim: Motor-excited granule cells had graded responses correlated with swim strength and could reach high instantaneous firing frequencies of up to 150 Hz during a fictive bout.
source: These granule cells had graded responses correlated with swim strength and could reach high instantaneous firing frequencies of up to 150 Hz during a fictive bout, similar to the burst firing seen in mammalian granule cells during locomotion (Powell et al., 2015) or whisker stimulation (van Beugen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on analysis of electrophysiological data and supported by citations.

claim: Half of motor-excited granule cells (N = 3/6) showed significant autocorrelations in their spiking activity during fictive swimming (p<0.001).
source: Half of these motor-excited granule cells (N = 3/6) also showed significant autocorrelations in their spiking activity during fictive swimming (p<0.001, Ljung-Box Q-test; Figure 6e).
evidence: This is based on autocorrelation analysis of electrophysiological data with statistical testing.

claim: The frequency of the spike autocorrelations for autocorrelated granule cells was comparable to the fictive swim frequency obtained from the ventral root (mean difference in frequency = 1.3 ± 0.6 Hz).
source: The frequency of the spike autocorrelations for these cells was comparable to the fictive swim frequency obtained from the ventral root (mean difference in frequency = 1.3 ± 0.6 Hz, N = 3), suggesting that the periodicity of granule cell spiking is related to the swimming activity (Figure 6e).
evidence: This is based on comparison of autocorrelation frequencies between granule cell spikes and ventral root activity.

claim: Motor efference copies are relayed along mossy fibers to many granule cells to drive burst firing during swimming bouts, whether fictive or real.
source: Together, these results suggest that motor efference copies are relayed along mossy fibers to many granule cells to drive burst firing during swimming bouts, whether fictive or real.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the granule cell electrophysiology and imaging data.

claim: Parallel fibers deliver graded swim-related excitation to nearly all cerebellar Purkinje cells.
source: In turn, parallel fibers deliver graded swim-related excitation to nearly all cerebellar Purkinje cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the granule cell and Purkinje cell data.

claim: The widespread increases in Purkinje cell calcium signals observed during swimming likely reflect simple spike bursts in Purkinje cells driven by the high frequency firing of one or more presynaptic granule cells carrying motor efference information.
source: The widespread increases in Purkinje cell calcium signals observed in the behaving animal during swimming (Figure 2a,b) therefore are likely to reflect simple spike bursts in Purkinje cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) driven by the high frequency firing of one or more presynaptic granule cells carrying motor efference information.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the imaging and electrophysiology data.

claim: As a population, Purkinje cells preferentially encode visual features in their complex spike activity whereas swimming activity is predominantly encoded by simple spikes.
source: Our data suggests that as a population, Purkinje cells preferentially encode visual features in their complex spike activity whereas swimming activity, arriving in the form of motor efference copies, is predominantly encoded by simple spikes.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the electrophysiological data analysis.

claim: Purkinje cells belonging to the three different visual complex spike phenotypes have simple spike activity that is correlated most strongly with motor activity (fraction of total signal from motor regressors = 0.65 ± 0.05, 0.54 ± 0.07, 0.76 ± 0.02).
source: Breaking this down by group, we find that Purkinje cells belonging to the three different visual complex spike phenotypes described above have simple spike activity that is correlated most strongly with motor activity (fraction of total signal from motor regressors = 0.65 ± 0.05, 0.54 ± 0.07, 0.76 ± 0.02 for the three visual complex spike phenotypes; Figure 7—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is based on multilinear regression analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: For Purkinje cells with dominant motor-related complex spike phenotypes, the contribution of motor activity to simple spike activity is relatively low (0.35 ± 0.12) and simple spikes are instead broadly influenced by a combination of sensory and motor features.
source: In contrast, for the small group of Purkinje cells with dominant motor-related complex spike phenotypes, the contribution of motor activity to simple spike activity is relatively low (0.35 ± 0.12) and simple spikes are instead broadly influenced by a combination of sensory and motor features (Figure 7—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is based on multilinear regression analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: Sensory and motor information is preferentially combined in Purkinje cells from distinct sources.
source: Together, these data suggest that sensory and motor information is preferentially combined in Purkinje cells from distinct sources.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the analysis of complex spike and simple spike contributions.

claim: Complex spikes typically cause a brief pause of tens of milliseconds in simple spike firing that can be followed by an increase or decrease in simple spikes lasting hundreds of milliseconds.
source: On a short timescale, complex spikes typically cause a brief pause of tens of milliseconds in simple spike firing that can be followed by an increase or decrease in simple spikes lasting hundreds of milliseconds.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cerebellar physiology.

claim: The particular complex spike-triggered change in simple spiking is robust for a given Purkinje cell but varies considerably across cells.
source: The particular complex spike-triggered change in simple spiking is robust for a given Purkinje cell but varies considerably across cells (Zhou et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2015; Xiao et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Heterogeneity was observed in the relationship between complex and simple spikes across Purkinje cell recordings.
source: Similar to previous findings, we observed heterogeneity in the relationship between complex and simple spikes across Purkinje cell recordings (Figure 7a).
evidence: This is based on analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: No clear spatial organization of the complex spike-simple spike relationship was observed in this dataset.
source: Previous studies have suggested that the modulation of simple spike firing by a complex spike is related to the cell's location within the cerebellum (Zhou et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2015). We did not, however, observe any clear spatial organization of the complex spike-simple spike relationship in this dataset (Figure 7a).
evidence: This is based on analysis of electrophysiological data and comparison with literature.

claim: The relationship between a complex spike and the simple spike firing rate was similar whether or not visual stimuli were being presented during periods when the fish was at rest.
source: In periods during which the fish was at rest (no fictive swimming), the relationship between a complex spike and the simple spike firing rate was similar whether or not visual stimuli were being presented (Figure 7b, 'non-motor' versus 'blank trials').
evidence: This is based on analysis of electrophysiological data under different conditions.

claim: When the fish was performing a fictive swim bout, the effect of a complex spike on simple spike output appeared diminished.
source: When the fish was performing a fictive swim bout however, the effect of a complex spike on simple spike output appeared diminished (Figure 7b, 'non-motor' versus 'motor'), which was not the case for complex spikes occurring during a cell's preferred complex spike sensory stimulus versus those occurring during all other periods (Figure 7b, 'pref. sensory' versus 'all other periods').
evidence: This is based on analysis of electrophysiological data under different behavioral conditions.

claim: The acute effect of a complex spike to modulate simple spike rates was identical between motor and non-motor periods for only a 50 millisecond period following the complex spike.
source: Upon closer examination of the temporal window around the occurrence of a complex spike, we observed that the acute effect of a complex spike to modulate simple spike rates was identical between motor and non-motor periods for only a 50 millisecond period following the complex spike, after which time simple spiking returned to high levels correlated with ongoing behavior (Figure 7c,d).
evidence: This is based on detailed temporal analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: The temporal window of complex spike effect on simple spikes was the same across cells regardless of whether the baseline modulation by a complex spike was to pause or facilitate simple spike firing.
source: This temporal window was the same across cells regardless of whether the baseline modulation by a complex spike was to pause or facilitate simple spike firing.
evidence: This is based on analysis of electrophysiological data across different cell types.

claim: The acute effect of a complex spike to change simple spike output in a Purkinje cell is temporally restricted by the behavioral state of the animal.
source: These findings suggest that the acute effect of a complex spike to change simple spike output in a Purkinje cell is temporally restricted by the behavioral state of the animal and that plasticity mechanisms relying on coincident complex spike and simple spike activity will have a unique dependence on motor context (see discussion).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the analysis of complex spike-simple spike interactions under different behavioral conditions.

claim: Plasticity mechanisms relying on coincident complex spike and simple spike activity will have a unique dependence on motor context.
source: These findings suggest that the acute effect of a complex spike to change simple spike output in a Purkinje cell is temporally restricted by the behavioral state of the animal and that plasticity mechanisms relying on coincident complex spike and simple spike activity will have a unique dependence on motor context (see discussion).
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings about motor context effects.
